Estimate the hybrid history of sampled populations

Source: R/estimate.R
estimate_history.Rd

Gives one answer per population, from one of two tiers:

  • Individual classes. When most hybrids confidently fit an early class (F1, F2, first or second backcross; see classify_hybrids()) and those are mostly F1s and backcrosses rather than F2-like animals, the ages follow directly from the classes: F1 = 1, first backcross = 1.5, second backcross = 1.75, F2 = 2 generations (hybrid age, both species), and likewise for the rare species' lines and the number of backcrosses. Intervals come from resampling animals, widened to at least the error of class-based ages in the reference at a similar share of early hybrids.

  • Population clock. Otherwise the trained clock is used: the sample's summaries are compared with the simulated reference.

Usage

estimate_history(
  clock,
  scores,
  population,
  diag = NULL,
  shared = NULL,
  markers = NULL,
  positions = NULL,
  effective_markers = NULL,
  het_dropout = 0,
  repeats = 30,
  seed = 1
)

Arguments

clock

Output of train_clock().

scores

Output of hybrid_scores() (columns S, H, n_markers).

population

Population label of each animal.

diag

Genotypes at the diagnostic markers (orient_genotypes()), needed if the reference used them (it always does).

shared

Genotypes at shared loci, needed if the reference had shared loci.

markers, effective_markers, het_dropout

No longer used, kept so that older scripts run. The classes that decide between the two tiers are made exactly as in the reference (from S, H and the number of markers, with default settings), so that the rule learned on the reference applies; use classify_hybrids() with these settings for the individual calls.

positions

Marker positions matching the columns of diag (chromosome, position), needed if the reference used a fixed map.

repeats

Number of random subsets for larger populations.

seed

Random seed.

Value

A data.frame with one row per population: n, n_hybrids (animals not classified as pure), rare_species (the species with less ancestry in the hybrids), rare_share (its mean share in the hybrids), method, early_share (share of hybrids in early classes), an estimate and interval (_lower, _upper) for hybrid_age_both, hybrid_age_rare and backcrosses, the arrival probability arriving and rate arrival_rate (always from the clock), and notes. arriving_note flags young swarms (hybrid age under 5 generations), where pure founders of the rarer species still form new hybrids without any arrivals and the arrival call was right only 63-67% of the time in validation. information is 1 minus the width of the hybrid-age interval relative to the spread of ages in the reference (log scale): near 1 the data pin the age down, near 0 the answer mostly reflects the reference's age range (few or weak markers), and note says so. note also flags populations with too few hybrids.

Details

F2-like animals are not trusted as second-generation hybrids on their own: in a swarm that mates among itself, F3, F4 and later generations have the same expected hybrid index and heterozygosity as F2s, so one animal cannot show its generation. Only the population can, through linkage blocks that shrink and drift that accumulates over generations, which is what the clock reads.

The share of hybrids in early classes at which the answer switches to the classes was chosen when the clock was trained, as the point above which the classes' large errors (90th percentile) on held-out simulated histories were no worse than the clock's, or under about 30%. With few or weak markers, later-generation animals still fit early classes, so the classes are never used. Column method says which tier gave the answer; the other tier's estimates are kept in columns starting clock_ and classes_.

Populations sampled more heavily than the reference are summarized in random subsets of the reference sample size and the results averaged (on the model's scale), so that every summary is computed exactly as in training.

Examples

# \donttest{
ex <- hybridclock_example()
mk <- diagnostic_markers(ex$genotypes, ex$groups, "species1", "species2", locus = ex$locus)
sc <- hybrid_scores(ex$genotypes, mk)
ref <- build_reference(n_sims = 150, generations = 12, n_markers = nrow(mk),
                       breeders = c(20, 100))
clock <- train_clock(ref, targets = "hybrid_age_both", committees = 5)
hyb <- ex$groups %in% c("site_A", "site_B")
estimate_history(clock, sc[hyb, ], ex$groups[hyb], diag = orient_genotypes(ex$genotypes, mk)[hyb, ])
#>   population  n n_hybrids rare_species rare_share           method early_share
#> 1     site_A 30        30     species2  0.4427813 population clock   0.5666667
#> 2     site_B 30        30     species2  0.1213907 population clock   0.1000000
#>   f2_share hybrid_age_both hybrid_age_both_lower hybrid_age_both_upper note
#> 1        1        4.066974              2.667928              5.859943     
#> 2        0        5.867665              3.774258              8.599688     
#>   classes_hybrid_age_both classes_hybrid_age_both_lower
#> 1                    2.00                      1.809675
#> 2                    1.75                      1.583465
#>   classes_hybrid_age_both_upper clock_hybrid_age_both
#> 1                      2.210342              4.066974
#> 2                      1.934049              5.867665
#>   clock_hybrid_age_both_lower clock_hybrid_age_both_upper information
#> 1                    2.667928                    5.859943   0.6529643
#> 2                    3.774258                    8.599688   0.6367845
# }
